title: LDL oxidation and cerebrovascular aging: mechanisms of endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and vascular cognitive impairment and dementia

sections.abstract:
Vascular cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID) is increasingly recognized as one of the leading causes of cognitive decline in aging populations. VCID is driven by the interplay of endothelial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation. Aging exacerbates cerebrovascular damage by impairing endothelial function, compromising the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and promoting neuroinflammation, all of which contribute to the progression of small vessel disease (SVD) and white matter hyperintensities (WMHs), which are hallmarks of VCID. Epidemiological evidence suggests that aging is associated with modifications in circulating low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and high-density lipoproteins (HDL), particularly oxidation, which further accelerates neurovascular pathology. Oxidized LDL (oxLDL) disrupts endothelial homeostasis, enhances leukocyte adhesion, and triggers chronic inflammatory signaling through microglial and astrocytic activation. Additionally, oxLDL-mediated oxidative stress exacerbates mitochondrial dysfunction and epigenetic alterations in cerebrovascular cells, reinforcing a cycle of vascular injury and neurodegeneration. These mechanisms contribute to neurovascular uncoupling, cerebral hypoperfusion, and cognitive decline in aging individuals. This review examines the pathophysiological role of oxLDL in VCID, with a focus on its impact on endothelial integrity, BBB function, neuroinflammation, and lipid-mediated neurodegenerative processes. Furthermore, we discuss emerging therapeutic strategies targeting LDL oxidation, inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction as potential interventions to mitigate the burden of VCID in aging populations.

Keywords: Oxidized LDL (oxLDL), Cerebrovascular aging, Endothelial dysfunction, Neuroinflammation, Vascular cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID)
sections.introduction:
Aging and hyperlipidemia are two major risk factors for vascular cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID) in the elderly, yet their combined effects on cerebrovascular function remain poorly understood. Among modifiable vascular risk factors, hypertension consistently demonstrates the strongest association with cerebral small vessel disease, white matter hyperintensities, and vascular dementia, with midlife hypertension conferring approximately a 1.5–2-fold increased risk of later-life dementia in large longitudinal cohorts [ 1 , 2 ]. Diabetes and metabolic syndrome are also associated with increased dementia risk, typically in the range of 1.3–1.6-fold depending on cohort and duration of exposure [ 3 ]. By comparison, midlife hypercholesterolemia has been linked to a more modest but significant increase in dementia incidence, with meta-analyses suggesting that each ∼1 mmol/L elevation in LDL-C is associated with approximately 5–10% higher dementia risk [ 4 ]. Aging itself remains the dominant non-modifiable determinant of cognitive decline, interacting synergistically with vascular exposures [ 1 ]. While hypertension likely carries the greatest population-attributable risk for VCID, hyperlipidemia, and particularly LDL oxidation, may represent a mechanistically distinct and modifiable contributor to microvascular dysfunction through pathways involving oxidative stress, endothelial senescence, and blood–brain barrier vulnerability. While aging leads to progressive cerebrovascular dysfunction through endothelial senescence [ 5 ], oxidative stress [ 6 ], neuroinflammation [ 7 ], and impaired autoregulation [ 8 ], hyperlipidemia exacerbates these processes by promoting vascular lipid deposition [ 9 ], systemic inflammation, and increased production of oxidized lipids [ 10 ] ( Fig. 1 ). Despite their individual contributions to cognitive decline, the synergistic mechanisms through which aging and dyslipidemia accelerate neurovascular damage remain understudied, leaving critical gaps in our understanding of their interplay in the pathogenesis of age-related VCID. The aging vasculature undergoes profound structural and functional changes, including decreased endothelial function [ 11 ], increased arterial stiffness [ 12 ], reduced nitric oxide (NO) bioavailability [ 13 ], and chronic low-grade inflammation [ 14 ], that impair cerebral blood flow (CBF) regulation [ 8 , 15 , 16 ] and contribute to blood–brain barrier (BBB) breakdown [ 8 , 17 ]. In parallel, hyperlipidemia induces vascular oxidative stress and inflammation through mechanisms involving LDL oxidation, foam cell formation, and dysregulated lipid metabolism [ 18 ]. Recent data indicate that small dense LDL particles have higher atherogenic potential and greater susceptibility to oxidation than larger LDL [ 19 ], while electronegative LDL (L5) has been linked to cognitive impairment in human studies [ 20 ]. These harmful subfractions may disproportionately contribute to cerebrovascular injury in aging. Although the separate impacts of aging and dyslipidemia on cerebrovascular health are well-established, the molecular pathways through which they synergistically damage the neurovascular unit (NVU) remain largely unexplored. LDL and its oxidized form, oxLDL, are increasingly recognized as central mediators of cerebrovascular aging and disease [ 21 ]. Despite the brain's own cholesterol metabolism, aging-associated BBB vulnerability permits infiltration of oxLDL into the CNS, compromising cerebrovascular function [ 22 ]. Peripheral dyslipidemia can thus exert profound effects on cerebral endothelial health [ 23 ]. It is important to clarify that under physiological conditions, circulating LDL and oxLDL do not freely cross the BBB [ 24 ]. The adult brain relies primarily on locally synthesized cholesterol, and BBB endothelial cells maintain highly regulated transport systems that restrict nonspecific lipoprotein entry. Therefore, oxLDL access to the central nervous system is not a physiological process. Rather, exposure of the NVU to circulating oxLDL occurs predominantly in the context of BBB dysfunction, which may arise from aging, hypertension, metabolic disease, inflammation, or cerebral small vessel pathology. Age-associated endothelial senescence, tight junction disorganization, and increased caveolar or vesicular transcytosis create permissive conditions that allow plasma-derived factors, including modified lipoproteins, to access the perivascular space and potentially the parenchyma. Much of the experimental evidence demonstrating oxLDL accumulation in brain tissue derives from models with established barrier impairment, such as hyperlipidemic or LDL receptor–deficient mice, ischemic injury models, or other pathological states, rather than from healthy, intact systems. Elevated LDL, and especially oxLDL, harms the brain microvasculature by promoting BBB breakdown, chronic inflammation, and neurodegeneration [ 25 ]. OxLDL induces endothelial dysfunction, increases barrier permeability, and enhances monocyte adhesion and microglial activation [ 18 ]. Mechanistic studies highlight lectin-like oxidized LDL receptor-1 (LOX-1) as a key receptor in oxLDL signaling within endothelial cells, promoting NF-κB activation, oxidative stress, and BBB disruption in aged animals [ 26 ]. Moreover, proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9), beyond regulating LDL receptor recycling, mediates inflammatory responses and oxLDL uptake, representing another age-dependent driver of neurovascular dysfunction [ 27 ]. Despite this growing evidence, longitudinal and mechanistic studies exploring chronic dyslipidemia's impact on cerebrovascular aging and cognition remain sparse. Current therapeutic strategies for managing hyperlipidemia focus primarily on lowering the amount of cholesterol carried within LDL (LDL-C), with statins serving as the cornerstone of both primary and secondary prevention. While these agents effectively reduce LDL-C levels and lower the incidence of major cardiovascular events, a substantial proportion of patients continue to experience adverse vascular outcomes, highlighting the existence of residual risk. This has prompted growing interest in the role of modified lipoproteins, particularly oxidized and electronegative forms of LDL, which exert potent pro-inflammatory and pro-atherogenic effects independent of LDL-C concentration. While VCID and AD are often discussed together, they are mechanistically distinct entities that frequently coexist in aging populations. VCID is primarily driven by cerebrovascular pathology, including small vessel disease, BBB disruption, endothelial dysfunction, hypoperfusion, and white matter injury, whereas AD is neuropathologically defined by amyloid-β plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles. However, these conditions share convergent pathways such as oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and BBB breakdown. In this context, oxLDL-mediated vascular injury most directly aligns with the vascular axis of cognitive decline and VCID pathogenesis through endothelial dysfunction, LOX-1 signaling, and neurovascular uncoupling. Its contribution to AD is likely indirect, acting as a vascular amplifier that may impair amyloid clearance, disrupt APOE-mediated lipid handling, and lower the threshold for neurodegenerative processes in mixed dementia states. This review synthesizes recent high-impact research on LDL/oxLDL effects in brain endothelial cells, focusing on BBB integrity, vascular aging, and links to Alzheimer's disease (AD) and VCID. We explore the synergy between aging and dyslipidemia in accelerating brain endothelial injury and subsequent cognitive decline, summarize preclinical and clinical advancements, including emerging therapeutic interventions, and discuss experimental models, controversies, and future directions for targeting LDL/oxLDL-mediated neurovascular dysfunction. Throughout this review, the term “elevated” or “high” LDL is used with explicit contextual definition. In human studies, elevated LDL-C refers to clinically recognized thresholds (e.g., ≥130 mg/dL [3.4 mmol/L] as borderline high and ≥160 mg/dL [4.1 mmol/L] as high). In murine models, however, LDL levels depend strongly on genotype and diet. ApoE −/− and Ldlr −/− mice maintained on standard chow exhibit moderately elevated circulating cholesterol relative to wild-type controls, whereas Western or high-fat diet feeding markedly amplifies LDL and total cholesterol levels, often several-fold above wild-type values. Accordingly, when referencing these models, we specify whether hyperlipidemia is genetically driven, diet-induced, or relative to wild-type comparators to avoid ambiguity and improve translational clarity across species (see Table 1 ).

Synergistic mechanisms linking aging, dyslipidemia, and neurovascular dysfunction in vascular cognitive impairment. This conceptual diagram illustrates how aging and dyslipidemia converge to drive progressive neurovascular dysfunction and cognitive decline through multiple interconnected pathways. On the left side, aging promotes oxidative stress through elevated reactive oxygen species production, endothelial dysfunction characterized by reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, mitochondrial impairment with increased mtROS and reduced oxidative phosphorylation, and blood-brain barrier leakiness due to loss of tight junction protein integrity. On the right side, dyslipidemia drives low-density lipoprotein accumulation in circulation, which undergoes oxidative modification to form oxidized LDL. OxLDL formation creates a pro-oxidant, pro-inflammatory milieu that further promotes oxidative stress and triggers activation of the lectin-like oxidized LDL receptor-1 (LOX-1) on endothelial cells, leading to increased intracellular ROS production and mitochondrial dysfunction. Together, these processes synergistically disrupt the neurovascular unit, comprising endothelial cells, pericytes, astrocytes, and neurons, causing multiple deleterious effects: (1) BBB breakdown with loss of tight junction proteins (claudin-5, occludin, and zonula occludens-1/ZO-1) and increased vascular permeability, (2) impaired neurovascular coupling due to reduced NO bioavailability and defective endothelium-dependent vasodilation, and (3) white matter injury characterized by demyelination and axonal loss. These pathological changes culminate in cerebral hypoperfusion, chronic neuroinflammation, and ultimately vascular cognitive impairment and dementia.

Mechanistic pathways linking oxLDL to cerebrovascular dysfunction and VCID. This table summarizes major biological mechanisms through which oxLDL contributes to cerebrovascular injury and cognitive decline. OxLDL promotes endothelial activation and dysfunction through scavenger receptor signaling, oxidative stress, and reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, leading to impaired vasodilation and neurovascular coupling. In parallel, oxLDL induces mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance in vascular cells, exacerbating energetic stress within the neurovascular unit. These processes contribute to blood–brain barrier disruption, inflammatory activation of vascular and glial cells, and structural remodeling of small cerebral vessels.

sections.conclusion:
Converging evidence indicates that the interplay of aging, LDL, and especially oxLDL is a critical driver of cerebrovascular injury underlying VCID. Epidemiological studies have demonstrated that midlife hypercholesterolemia is associated with an increased risk of dementia, with each ∼1 mmol/L rise in LDL levels linked to an estimated 8% higher incidence of all-cause dementia [ 167 , 168 ]. Mechanistically, atherosclerosis-prone conditions like high LDL promote intracranial arterial disease that compromises cerebral perfusion and precipitates ischemic injury [ 169 ]. Beyond large vessels, cholesterol and its oxidized derivatives can accumulate in the cerebral microvasculature, inciting local inflammation and neurodegeneration [ 169 ]. In the aging brain, these processes are compounded by an intrinsically fragile vasculature, establishing a strong case that aging, LDL, and oxLDL must be studied synergistically in the context of brain microvascular health and VCID pathogenesis. OxLDL emerges as a particularly deleterious player within the NVU. Once native LDL particles undergo oxidation, they trigger endothelial dysfunction more potently than native LDL [ 94 ]. OxLDL engages endothelial cells to upregulate adhesion molecules and pro-inflammatory pathways, while directly degrading the integrity of the endothelial barrier [ 82 , 83 ]. This damage to the BBB permits leakage of neurotoxic blood-derived factors into the brain parenchyma [ 170 ], exacerbating oxidative stress and inflammation within brain tissue. Indeed, oxLDL creates a vicious cycle: it is readily taken up by macrophages and brain glia, generating foam cells and further ROS and cytokine release [ 18 , 85 , 94 , 171 ]. The result is chronic neurovascular inflammation, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability (impairing vasodilation), and breakdown of microvascular structure, changes that manifest as small vessel disease, microhemorrhages, and ultimately cognitive impairment. Thus, aging-related oxidative stress and oxLDL together destabilize the BBB and cerebral perfusion, linking peripheral dyslipidemia to the hallmark microvascular lesions of VCID. These insights also highlight emerging gaps and complexities. For example, lipid-laden microglia and perivascular macrophages observed in aged or diseased brains mirror the foam cells of peripheral atherosclerosis [ 169 ], suggesting common pathways yet underscoring that the brain's unique environment (e.g. BBB selectivity and glial responses) may modulate disease expression. Clinical data on blood lipids and cognition have sometimes been inconsistent, with some cohorts even hint at a U-shaped relationship wherein very low cholesterol might impair neuronal function while high cholesterol clearly promotes vascular injury [ 172 ]. This paradox emphasizes that simply measuring LDL levels is not enough; the quality of lipids (e.g. propensity to oxidize) and the context of aging are pivotal. Unresolved mechanisms include precisely how oxLDL interacts with other dementia-related processes (such as amyloid-β accumulation or APOE4-mediated lipid dysregulation) in driving cognitive decline. Addressing these open questions will require translational studies that integrate vascular biology with geroscience, to unravel how age-related lipid toxicity intersects with neurodegenerative cascades in VCID.

Importantly, the detrimental effects of oxLDL point to the need for targeted therapeutic strategies beyond standard LDL-cholesterol reduction. LDL-lowering therapies (e.g. statins) reduce cardiovascular events, but many patients on optimal therapy still experience cerebrovascular complications, a “residual risk” driven in part by ongoing vascular inflammation and oxidative damage [ 173 , 174 ]. In the brain, this residual risk may manifest as continued BBB disruption and microvascular damage despite controlled plasma LDL, because oxLDL and its downstream inflammatory sequelae remain unmitigated. Therefore, future interventions should aim to neutralize oxLDL's harmful actions on the cerebral vasculature. Approaches could include enhancing antioxidant defenses or upregulating endothelial-protective factors to prevent LDL oxidation and endothelial activation. Notably, experimental evidence shows that boosting endothelial expression of anti-inflammatory transcription factors (such as KLF2) can ameliorate oxLDL-induced dysfunction [ 82 , 167 ], illustrating a viable strategy to preserve endothelial health. Another avenue is to inhibit oxLDL's receptors (e.g. LOX-1) or GPER and Scavenger Receptor Class B Type 1 (SR-BI) on brain endothelial cells [ 175 ], thereby blocking the cascade of leukocyte adhesion, ROS generation, and tight-junction disruption that follows oxLDL exposure. Enhancing the beneficial arm of lipid transport, for instance, raising HDL or improving its functionality, may also help, as higher HDL is associated with better cognitive outcomes in older adults [ 167 ]. By addressing the inflammatory and oxidative components of vascular aging, such therapies would tackle the root causes of ongoing microvascular injury. Recent work further refines the concept of the “leaky” aging BBB by demonstrating that age-related dysfunction is not limited to tight junction disruption but also involves altered endothelial transport dynamics. Studies from Wyss-Coray and colleagues show that aging is associated with increased nonspecific vesicular transcytosis alongside reduced efficiency of selective transporter systems, shifting the BBB from a tightly regulated interface to a more permissive and dysregulated state [ 176 , 177 ]. This transport imbalance provides a mechanistic framework by which circulating factors, including modified lipoproteins, may gain enhanced access to perivascular compartments under aging conditions, even prior to overt structural barrier breakdown. Taken together, these findings suggest that aging, increased circulating LDL, and thus oxidized LDL form a pathological triad that accelerates cerebrovascular damage and cognitive decline. The cumulative literature synthesized here supports the thesis that these factors must be interrogated in concert in future VCID research, with particular attention to their impact on the brain's microvasculature. Recognizing oxLDL as a mediator of residual vascular risk underscores a paradigm shift: successful prevention of VCID will likely require interventions that go beyond lowering LDL alone. Targeting oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and neuroinflammation fueled by oxLDL is an auspicious strategy to protect the aging brain's blood vessels. Such an approach – in tandem with traditional risk factor control, may hold promise to reduce the burden of vascular cognitive impairment and dementia in our increasingly aged population, ultimately translating mechanistic insights into preventive and therapeutic breakthroughs.
